title: One bubble tea, half sugar
title_target: 一杯珍珠奶茶，半糖少冰
goal: Order food and drinks with exactly the sugar and ice you like — and get past the biggest wall for English speakers: measure words.
bekal: use measure words correctly and know the way out when you forget
order a drink with sugar and ice levels like a Taiwanese
tell 吃 from 喝 and use 要 to order

dialogs.title: 對話 — 手搖飲料店
dialogs.intro: A hot afternoon. Budi and Xiaomei stop at the tea shop across from campus.

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.id: Welcome! What would you like to drink?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [我要|Wǒ yào][一杯|yì bēi][珍珠奶茶|zhēnzhū nǎichá]，[大杯|dà bēi]。
lines.id: I'd like one bubble tea, large.
lines.literal: I — want — one — cup — pearl — milk-tea, big — cup.

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.id: How sweet, and how much ice?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.literal: half — sugar, less — ice, thank thank.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Um… I don't know how to say it.
lines.literal: um… I — not — know — how — say.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: It's his first time. Just give him the same.
lines.literal: he — first — time — drink. give — him — one-same — (one) — (OK).

lines.speaker: 店員:
lines.text: [沒問題|Méi wèntí]。[兩杯|Liǎng bēi][一共|yígòng][一百三|yìbǎi sān]。
lines.id: No problem. Two cups, that's 130 altogether.
lines.literal: not — have — problem. two — cup — altogether — hundred-three.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [我|Wǒ][請客|qǐngkè]！[小美|Xiǎoměi][幫|bāng][我|wǒ][這麼多|zhème duō]。
lines.id: My treat! Xiaomei, you've helped me so much.
lines.literal: I — invite-guest! Xiaomei — help — me — this — much.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: No need! You can treat me next time.
lines.literal: not — need — (la)! below — time — you — invite.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [那|Nà][我們|wǒmen][也|yě][吃|chī][點|diǎn][東西|dōngxi][好嗎|hǎo ma]？
lines.id: Then shall we get something to eat too?
lines.literal: then — we — also — eat — a-little — thing — good — (question)?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [好啊|Hǎo a]！[隔壁|Gébì][有|yǒu][很好吃|hěn hǎochī][的|de][滷肉飯|lǔròufàn]。
lines.id: Sure! Next door does really good braised pork rice.
lines.literal: good — (ah)! next-door — have — very — tasty — (one) — braised-meat-rice.

lines.text: [您的|Nín de][飲料|yǐnliào][好了|hǎo le]！[謝謝|Xièxie][光臨|guānglín]！

lines.literal: you — 's — drink — good — (done)! thank thank — light-come!

notes: ⚠️ **手搖飲料 ("hand-shaken drinks") is one of the most Taiwanese things there is.** There are tens of thousands of shops across the island, and almost all of them ask the same two questions: sugar level and ice level. Not answering brings the line to a halt.

**請客 means to treat someone**, literally "invite a guest". ⚠️ In Taiwan the person who suggests going out usually pays, and refusing once or twice before accepting is part of good manners. Splitting the bill evenly is called **AA制** (*AA zhì*).
**好嗎？ and 好啊！ are a pair.** 好嗎 softens a suggestion into a question ("…OK?"), and 好啊 is a warm yes. Answering with a bare 好 sounds flat, almost reluctant.

**滷肉飯 (*lǔròufàn*) is Taiwan's national dish** — rice topped with small pieces of pork slow-braised in soy sauce. A small bowl costs about 30–40 塊. ⚠️ If you don't eat pork, say *我不吃豬肉* (*wǒ bù chī zhūròu*); the safe choice is 素食 (*sùshí*, vegetarian food), which is very easy to find in Taiwan.
**歡迎光臨 is called out every time a shop door opens.** You don't need to reply at all.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Measure words: the wall you have to get over now
body: This is the number-one mistake for English speakers, and the reason makes sense: English **has** measure words (a cup of tea, a piece of paper) but **skips them** for most nouns — "three books", "two people". Mandarin gives you no such freedom.
The rule is one sentence: **between a number (or 這/那/幾) and the noun there MUST be a measure word.**
after: **The way out when you forget: use 個 (*ge*).** It is the general measure word and is understood with almost anything. Using 個 where another word fits better sounds like an accent; **using no measure word at all** sounds like a robot.
⚠️ Note that **when the noun is clear from the conversation, the noun can disappear but the measure word can't**: *我要三個。* — "I'd like three."

grammars.title: The measure words you'll use most
body: You don't need to memorize them all today. The first ten rows of this table cover eighty percent of everyday conversation.

head: Measure word
Pīnyīn
Used for
Example
rows: 一杯奶茶 a cup of milk tea
兩碗飯 two bowls of rice
一份便當 one lunch box
一件衣服 a piece of clothing
一瓶水 a bottle of water

after: ⚠️ Remember the last unit's rule: before a measure word, two is **兩**, not 二. 兩杯, 兩個, 兩本.
**位 is the polite version of 個 for people.** Restaurant staff will greet you with *幾位？* ("how many people?"), and you answer *兩位* or simply *兩個*.

blocks.text: Two questions always come: **甜度** (sugar level) and **冰塊** (ice level). The answers come from a fixed list, and saying them in order — sugar first, then ice — is all you need.

blocks.title: A full order in one breath
items: **我要一杯珍珠奶茶，大杯，半糖少冰。** — One bubble tea, large, half sugar, light ice.
**中杯紅茶，微糖去冰，謝謝。** — Medium black tea, a little sugar, no ice, thanks.
**熱的拿鐵，無糖。** — Hot latte, no sugar.
⚠️ If you don't say anything, you'll get **全糖正常冰** — and Taiwanese milk tea with full sugar is far sweeter than you'd expect.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **吃 (*chī*, eat) and 喝 (*hē*, drink) can't be swapped** — English "eats" soup; Mandarin always says **喝湯** (drink soup). Anything liquid is drunk, no exceptions. And medicine is "eaten": **吃藥**, where English says "take".

⚠️ **內用還是外帶 is the question you'll hear most often in Taiwan** — at rice shops, drink stands, and 便利商店. Learn the two answers now: **內用** (for here) and **外帶** (to go). Answering with either one makes the whole transaction go smoothly.

items: I'd like a cup of milk tea.
